name: Savoy Music Center
writeup: Marc Savoy, born in 1940 and raised on a rice farm near Eunice, opened this shop on U.S. 190 east of town in 1966. He builds and repairs Cajun accordions here, sold under the Acadian name, and the store doubles as a meeting place for players. On most Saturday mornings, from nine until noon, musicians of all ages crowd in for a jam session that has become one of the best-known gatherings in Cajun music. The shop matters because it has kept handmade Louisiana accordions and the older dance repertoire within reach of new players.

name: Blue Moon Saloon and Guesthouse
writeup: The Blue Moon is a bar, stage and dance floor attached to a guesthouse at 215 East Convent Street in Lafayette's Freetown neighborhood. Mark Falgout has owned and run it since 2001, and it has become a regular stop for local and touring roots bands, with live Cajun music, a standing Cajun jam and heavy crowds during Festival International. Travelers staying in the guesthouse share the place with the dancers, which gives it a reputation as a honky-tonk where visitors and locals mix. In January 2025 the property was listed for sale at 1.2 million dollars.

name: El Sid O's Zydeco and Blues Club
writeup: Sid Williams, a St. Martinville native, opened this dance hall at 1523 North St. Antoine Street in 1984. His younger brother Nathan Williams started Nathan and the Zydeco Cha-Chas by playing Friday nights here, and Buckwheat Zydeco was a frequent performer in the club's early years; Clifton Chenier and Rockin' Dopsie also played the room. From 1986 Williams ran a Thanksgiving food drive from the club. He died on February 2, 2025, aged 73, and his family described El Sid O's as one of the last zydeco clubs still standing in Louisiana.

name: Wetlands Acadian Cultural Center
writeup: This National Park Service center on the bank of Bayou Lafourche, part of Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve, tells the story of the Acadians who settled Louisiana's bayous. It occupies the Percy-Lobdell Building, a 1907 grocery warehouse that was renovated and given a 200-seat theater before opening to the public in 1992. Music is part of the program: local players gather here for a free weekly Cajun music jam, held on Monday evenings, and the center has hosted outdoor Cajun and zydeco concerts. It gives the bayou parishes, east of the Cajun prairie, a public home for the music.

name: The Jolly Inn
writeup: The Jolly Inn on Barrow Street opened in 1998 and took its name from an older dance hall near Houma where founder Werlien Prosperie had gone with his parents as a boy and later played guitar and sang. Prosperie, who played accordion in a band called Couche Couche, built the new hall around live Cajun bands, and his daughter Sonia McNamara took it over. Dances on Friday nights and Sunday afternoons run through two-steps, waltzes, line dances and swamp pop. The family has said it may be the only dance hall left between New Orleans and Lafayette.

name: Iry LeJeune Marker
writeup: A roadside marker at 205 Rue Iry Lejeune, put up in 2021 by the William G. Pomeroy Foundation with the Center for Louisiana Studies, honors the accordionist born near Church Point in 1928. Nearly blind, LeJeune learned from his uncle Angelas LeJeune and took Amédé Ardoin as a model. His first record, made in Houston with fiddler Floyd LeBlanc, was followed by sides for Goldband in Lake Charles, among them "Love Bridge Waltz" and "Evangeline Special." They helped bring the accordion back to the front of Cajun bands after years of string-band fashion. He was killed in a roadside accident near Eunice on October 8, 1955. The year given is his birth.

name: Nellie Lutcher Memorial Park
writeup: Pianist and singer Nellie Lutcher was born in Lake Charles on October 15, 1912. At eight she was assistant pianist at New Sunlight Baptist Church; at twelve she joined her father, Isaac Lutcher, in Clarence Hart's Imperial Jazz Band and accompanied Ma Rainey. Signed to Capitol in 1947, she had hits with "Hurry on Down" and "Fine Brown Frame" and recorded "Lake Charles Boogie." She died in 2007. The city opened this park at 702 Enterprise Boulevard on November 3, 2023, with a stage edged in piano keys, and later added a mural of her. The year given is her birth; the park lies in the cultural district named for her.

name: Martin Accordions
writeup: Clarence "Junior" Martin, born in Cankton in 1940, was a home builder and a pedal steel guitarist who played with more than fifty bands. In 1983 he and his wife Patsy opened this workshop on West Willow Street, where the family builds ten-button, single-row diatonic accordions by hand and repairs and tunes instruments of every make. His daughter Pennye Huval and son Anthony work alongside, and the shop gives tours and demonstrations. Cajun and Creole players alike use Martin boxes; accordionist Corey Ledet has owned them for thirty years. Martin, a Louisiana Music Hall of Fame inductee, died in 2026 aged 85.

name: Mulate's (site)
writeup: Kerry Boutté, who grew up in Arnaudville, opened Mulate's in Breaux Bridge in 1980 and billed it as a Cajun restaurant when that label was still new. His idea was a fais do-do with a kitchen: gumbo, étouffée and fried seafood, and a live Cajun band every night. It became one of the area's biggest stages for Cajun music, and a second Mulate's later opened in New Orleans. On September 27, 2011, after 31 years, new owners renamed the Breaux Bridge original Pont Breaux's Cajun Restaurant and kept the nightly music; that restaurant, at 325 West Mills Avenue, has since closed.

name: Cajun French Music Hall of Fame and Museum
writeup: The Cajun French Music Association, a nonprofit founded in 1984 to promote and preserve Cajun music, keeps its hall of fame at 240 South C.C. Duson Street, a block from the Liberty Theatre. Its list of inductees begins in 1997, the year used here, and now runs past one hundred musicians nominated by the association's chapters. Inside are fiddles, accordions, guitars, hats and belts that belonged to them, some of the earliest Cajun records, and old dance hall advertisements. Many of those honored played on front porches and in small halls before the music was fashionable. Admission is free.
